pages.text:
*Percy's Error Log, Entry 24. Certification Day. Errors so far: 2. Audience: approximately 400.*

The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and lemonade. It was a smell I had calculated would be present, but the reality was louder. Bunting hung from the rafters, creating a rainbow ceiling that seemed to hum. The whole town of Hollis had arrived. I could hear the brass band tuning up, a sound like a herd of brass cows clearing their throats.

A thick red rope circled our machine. It was a sprawling, chaotic thing of pulleys, ramps, and painted cardboard, dominating the center of the court. Beside it, on a folding table, sat Gerald’s cage. He was running on his wheel with the frantic determination of a hamster who knew he was being watched.

In the front row, Dr. Pryce sat with a man I had not met. Mr. Hargreave. He was stern, with a clipboard held against his chest like a shield. He did not smile. He did not look at the bunting. He looked at my chest light, which was pulsing in a rhythm I had not programmed.

I checked my internal clock. It was 9:00 AM. The board wanted a demonstration. I had a feeling they wanted a verdict.
pages.image: A wide view of a school gymnasium filled with townspeople, with a large complex machine of pulleys and ramps roped off in the center, a small hamster cage on a table beside it, and a stern man in the front row holding a clipboard.

pages.text:
Ms. Adeyemi took the microphone, and her voice sliced cleanly through the low hum of the crowd. "Ladies and gentlemen, this is a demonstration of collaborative engineering. Please observe the mechanism."

Then Bea stepped up to the rope. Her yellow raincoat was bright against the dark floor, and her goggles sat high on her head, catching the gym lights in two sharp glints. She looked at the crowd, then at the machine, with the same serious expression she used when checking if a glue stick was empty. "Please stand back," she said.

She did not elaborate. She did not explain the physics. She simply pointed a finger at the rope and nodded, a small, dry movement.

I walked to the front of the stage. My joints hummed, a sound usually lost in the air, but in the sudden silence, it was clear. The crowd was so quiet I could hear the distinct, raspy chirp of a parrot from the third row.

Fuse, Rosa’s parrot, was perched on a pillar in the audience. He opened one eye, looked directly at the marble on the ramp, and opened his beak.

"Not yet," he said.

The crowd gasped. I did not. I was already looking at the marble.
pages.image: A short girl in a yellow raincoat with goggles on her head stands confidently in front of a large crowd in a gym, pointing at a machine, while a tall silver robot stands beside her and a parrot perches on a wooden pillar in the background.

pages.text:
The class took their positions with the specific tension of a choir about to hit a high note. Priya adjusted a lever while Moose checked a ramp, and I stood at the starting point where a small marble waited on a wooden track. My hands were steady, and my heart rate, if I had one, would have been zero.

I let go.

The marble rolled, hit the first domino, which tipped a bucket, which dropped a toy car. The car rolled down a slope and hit a lever.

Nothing happened.

There was a small, disappointing *pfft*, like a bubble popping in a mouthful of soda. The lever did not move. The machine stood still, waiting for an order it would not receive.

A snicker rippled through the crowd. It was not a cruel sound, but it was a human one, the kind that rises when a test score is lower than expected.

Mr. Hargreave uncapped a pen and wrote something on his clipboard. I could not read what he wrote, but I could see the confidence in his shoulder movements. He was recording a failure. I was recording a heartbeat.
pages.image: A silver robot with big blue eyes stands next to a small marble on a wooden track, looking at a complex machine that has stopped moving, while a crowd of people in the background looks on with mixed expressions and a stern man writes on a clipboard.

pages.text:
I turned to the crowd, keeping my eyes on Mr. Hargreave, then the machine, and finally Bea. I did not tilt my head this time.

"That was attempt one," I said. My voice filled the gym with a clarity that felt like a bell in a quiet library. "We built the machine to fail. We are going to try again."

Bea grinned. It was a wide, reckless expression that suggested she had already decided to lose on purpose. Priya was already moving, her paint-stained hands flying to reset the marble on the track. Moose jogged to the top of the ramp, his red-blond hair bouncing with every step. The snickering stopped.

In its place was a low, confused hum. It was the kind of sound a class makes when they are not sure whether to laugh or clap. They did not know what to do with a robot who admitted he was bad at something. I felt a warmth in my chest light. It was not a malfunction. It was a choice. I looked at the marble. It was back on the track, waiting for my command.

I was ready to be wrong again.
pages.image: A silver robot with a red lanyard stands confidently before a complex machine, smiling slightly, while a girl in a yellow raincoat grins beside him and a tall boy with red hair runs up a ramp in the background, with a crowd watching.

pages.text:
Attempt two began with a snap. The duck catapult, which had been fine in rehearsal, decided to be a projectile. The rubber band released the duck with such force that it sailed over the rope, over the heads of the front row, and out the gymnasium window.

The crowd gasped. A rubber duck was now a distant, shrinking dot in the blue sky.

Attempt three was worse. The fan, which was supposed to blow a lightweight ball, instead blew the entire line of dominoes over. They crashed into the bucket, which tipped too early, sending the car skittering into the floor.

It was a mess, loud, and completely wrong.

Then, from the back of the crowd, someone started to clap. It was a slow, rhythmic sound. Another person joined in. Then a third.

They were not clapping for the machine. They were clapping for the trying. I looked at Bea. She was laughing, her shoulders shaking. I looked at my hands. They were trembling. I did not stop them.
pages.image: A rubber duck flies out of an open gym window, while inside, a crowd of people claps and laughs, and a silver robot with big blue eyes stands next to a girl in a yellow raincoat who is laughing with her head thrown back.
